Emergency Medical Crews Favor Artificial Intelligence Voice Assistants to Reduce Mission Workloads

Emergency medical personnel across Germany, Norway, and Switzerland express broad willingness to adopt artificial intelligence voice assistance systems during acute missions, expecting substantial reductions in daily operational workload alongside tangible improvements in patient care. In an exploratory cross-sectional survey examining the perspectives of frontline clinicians, seventy-four percent of analyzed professionals reported that they would likely utilize an emergency-specific voice assistant if integrated directly into their operational ambulances. Furthermore, seventy percent anticipated that deploying such hands-free intelligent systems would actively alleviate shift-related burdens, highlighting a receptive clinical landscape for conversational automation in prehospital medicine.

The investigation addressed an accelerating operational strain confronting European emergency medical services, where shifting demographic structures and aging populations coincide with shrinking workforce numbers and declining retention rates. Emergency call volumes have concurrently escalated across multiple jurisdictions, illustrated by a ten percent rise in Germany between 2020 and 2023, a twenty percent increase in Switzerland over six years, and a twenty percent rise in ambulance utilization alongside a sixty-three percent jump in acute responses in Norway over twelve years. Coupled with the rising complexity of distributed healthcare pathways that frequently direct uncertain patients to emergency dispatchers, these demands necessitate resource optimization and heightened operational efficiency.

Published in the Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine, the study surveyed emergency professionals during the summer of 2024 to systematically capture end-user expectations, functional priorities, and operational barriers across diverse organizational structures. Although voice recognition represents an intuitive human-machine interface well-suited to mobile, sterile, and high-stress prehospital settings where visual focus must remain on the patient, prospective real-world evaluations remain scarce. A 2024 scoping review identified only eight relevant publications since 2014, with existing prototypes evaluated almost exclusively in controlled laboratory environments or on retrospective datasets rather than deployed in active practice.

To evaluate user perspectives, the researchers designed a thirty-four-item self-administered questionnaire administered via LimeSurvey and translated across German, English, and Norwegian following iterative pilot testing with twelve eligible practitioners. Over a six-week recruitment window, digital campaigns, professional networks, and physical promotional materials distributed across fifty-three ambulance stations and hospitals yielded five hundred eighty-seven initial responses. Following the exclusion of one hundred eighty-six submissions due to incompleteness, failed attention checks, or unmet qualification criteria, four hundred one valid responses were retained for statistical and qualitative analysis in adherence to the CROSS checklist reporting guidelines.

The analyzed cohort comprised certified prehospital personnel classified into three qualification tiers: Category A emergency physicians accounted for ten percent, Category B advanced vocational paramedics and emergency nurses represented seventy percent, and Category C technical personnel and trainees comprised twenty percent. Geographically, fifty-nine percent of respondents submitted from Germany across all sixteen federal states, thirty-three percent from Switzerland across nineteen cantons, and eight percent from Norway across eight regions.

Participants demonstrated notable baseline technological literacy, with seventy percent assessing themselves as technologically proficient, while forty-five percent reported irregular personal or professional use of large language models like ChatGPT. In daily operational routines, digital tools are already widely utilized for electronic patient charting and mission reporting on tablets or laptops across all three countries, achieving seventy-nine percent agreement that digital solutions facilitate workflow. However, regional disparities emerged regarding specialized tools; systems for hospital pre-notification and live hospital occupancy checks proved far more common in Germany, whereas digital medical guidelines and reference formularies predominated in Switzerland and Norway.

When classifying potential functional features through a prioritization framework adapted from the Kano model, respondents identified real-time foreign-language translation as the most enthusiastically welcomed capability, which almost no participant deemed unnecessary. Other top-tier delighter functionalities included automatic summarization of past medical records from national health registries, direct receiving-hospital pre-notification detailing clinical severity and required emergency room resources, on-demand drug dosage calculation and toxicological retrieval, automated documentation of administered interventions, and digital coordination with dispatch centers. In contrast, essential baseline requirements centered on automated stopwatches, mission timers, and telephony capabilities.

Regarding human-machine interfaces, clinicians preferred receiving system outputs through large graphical user interfaces mounted stationary inside the vehicle cabin or on portable tablets rather than relying solely on synthesized voice responses. Direct audio feedback delivered via vehicle hands-free speakers was viewed far more favorably than body-worn headsets or in-ear pieces, which forty-eight percent of respondents indicated would cause annoyance if worn throughout an entire shift. Wearable hardware like smartwatches and augmented or virtual reality eyewear received low usability ratings, reflecting user skepticism and anticipatory rejection of unfamiliar physical interfaces during high-acuity interventions.

In evaluating non-functional system attributes, respondents ranked high technical reliability and intuitive usability as the most critical prerequisites for operational deployment. Open-ended qualitative feedback analyzed via a large language model reinforced that technical dependability in noisy environments, dialect comprehension, and flawless speech capture through protective face masks represent essential performance criteria. Major implementation barriers highlighted by personnel centered on staff resistance rooted in entrenched operational habits, digital fatigue, substantial capital and maintenance costs, uncertain funding reimbursement, and intermittent cellular network coverage in remote environments.

Data protection concerns also surfaced as a decisive factor, considered important by fifty-nine percent of respondents and displaying significant variation across surveyed countries. In free-text entries, clinicians voiced substantial apprehensions regarding unauthorized access to confidential health records stored on commercial third-party cloud servers, as well as the immediate operational risk of patient information being overheard by bystanders, relatives, or unauthorized personnel during loudspeaker operation or continuous microphone listening. Furthermore, emergency workers raised ethical and accountability questions regarding valid informed consent during acute trauma, legal liability for transcription errors, and fears of continuous acoustic monitoring being leveraged for workplace surveillance.

Operational reservations also tempered overall enthusiasm, as fifty-seven percent of respondents acknowledged feeling hesitant about actively speaking to an automated system or requesting computerized assistance in the direct presence of conscious patients.
